speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head K of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The messaging and measures by the two Education Ministers on skills mastery, applied learning and broader school and IHL admission criteria are necessary in a landscape that has over-indulged in the academic paper chase.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, Sir, the relentless changes to the education and employment landscapes remain.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Technology and product and service lifecycles and shelf lives get shorter.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Anything that can be repeated and learnt by machines will be replaced by machines.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Futurists, such as Ray Kurzweil, predict that soon, a computer that cost US$1,000 will possess the cognitive capability of a human being by 2029.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On key education trends: the writing is on the wall.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just as in business, rapid changes are sweeping through the education landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Google "key education trends" and you will find at least 90% of the search results reflect key trends in the realm of technology − virtual reality, augmented reality, even mixed reality, cloud technology, learning analytics, coding and the Internet of Things (IoT).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Other trends include the move from Pedagogy (child-focused teaching approaches), to Andragogy (the study of teaching adults), to Heutagogy (self-directed learning); and from STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Math) to develop critical thinking and more creative approaches to problem solving.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How has MOE kept pace with these new education trends that are the outcome of rapid technological and economic disruptions?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How has the work of the Council for the Future Economy (CFE) and Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) affected the shape of education for students and educators?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When was the last time this has been reviewed and how does the prevailing work by CFE and Smart Nation change curriculum creation, development and assessment in schools and IHLs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the state of the SkillsFuture movement and what else can be done to urge Singaporeans to take even greater ownership and action to be ready for further disruptions in the labour market?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As all of the IHLs aggressively embark on Continuing Education and Training (CET), directed by MOE, potential overlapping and unnecessary competition are bound to emerge.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will MOE prevent this and instead enhance the synergy that can arise?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Would the Government even consider renaming MOE as the Ministry for Life-Long Learning to put the emphasis on lifelong and self-directed learning and remove barriers to learning for all citizens?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On the role of educators in the future world: the pervasiveness of mobile devices, such as smartphones, smart watches and tablets, has already overtaken desktop browsing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: M-learning, instead of e-learning, enables learners to access content even more freely.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Educators will need the technical and pedagogical support to integrate M-learning in their curricula.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a consultant told me, the role of educators is to think carefully now about the things that they typically do.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Minister update this House on how aware and prepared are our educators in their changing role in this new world of education?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What proportion of them are still in the mode of repeating lectures or rehearsing for high-stakes exams?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How have we equipped our educators to take on the role of designers of quality learning experiences, curators of content available online, creators of content and coaches of their students in matters of life?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Should there be an ITM as well for the educators to build the capability and deep skills of educators to keep pace with the needs of 21st century learners?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do educators of the future address skills deficits in the workforce and, if that is getting increasingly unpredictable, how do we prepare the students to acquire more learning agility to face the future?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On equal access to opportunities for all students: much has been spoken at last week's Budget Debate on inequality and/or inequity amongst citizens from low-income households versus others who are more affluent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst it is true that it is hard to ensure equality in life outcomes, it is certainly possible for the Government to do even more to ensure equal access to opportunities in learning and exposures that will further one's future readiness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But we need to also update and articulate the changing nature of the gaps in today's setting.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Holiday and/or enrichment programmes of children from more affluent backgrounds, for instance, have now moved from speech, drama and music lessons to the 21st century's coding, robotics, 3-D printing bootcamps and the like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A concern that has been raised globally is that of Digital Equity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can MOE please provide an update on what has been done in this aspect of digital equity?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On existing hot-button issues of over-emphasis on high-stakes exams and the tuition syndrome, it is not uncommon to tease parents whose children are taking the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) that they themselves are also taking the PSLE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not uncommon to still hear parents who are highly anxious and highly strung as they report that their children are taking the General Certificate of Education (GCE) examinations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The tuition industry is still a booming industry because doing well in high-stakes exams is still the ultimate aim of many parents and teachers of especially primary school and secondary school education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Her mother wrote to me, "Ms Phua, I am sharing this in the hope that it serves as an opportunity to point our education system to areas where we can do differently, to better cater to a wider spectrum of needs, as the time and tide have changed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although MOE has acknowledged Howard Gardner's work on multiple intelligences, our school system still leans towards our traditional definition of academic excellence".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we have improved in dealing with these hot button issues, why do many parents and students still fret incessantly over them?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could it be that it is insufficient to simply tweak the system through changes, such as PSLE banding instead of T-scores, by allowing subject combinations instead of removing the labels of Express, Normal (Academic) (NA) and Normal (Technical) (NT) and Special Schools?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Are we merely rearranging the chairs on the deck and not making deep enough changes?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In this age of disruptions, do we dare proactively disrupt our current education systems by slaying some of the sacred cows that we inherited from the proverbial third Industrial Revolution when we are already in the fourth?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have many times in this House shared on how we need to remove this structural thorn in the flesh of the system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are highly respected education systems globally which do not sort students at the age of 12.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I recall what a very dedicated MOE mainstream educator told me, and I quote, "Ms Phua, I know there are a lot of things to consider before we can abolish PSLE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the fact of the matter is − if you ask a teacher if he or she would teach differently in a class if there is no PSLE, I am quite sure the answer is a yes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are just not enough time and room to develop the skills they need to survive in the future world – skills like creativity, flexibility, 21st century competencies that MOE has been advocating.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need more time to look into non-examinable subjects, such as inquiry, discovering and development of strengths of our students".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Last year, at the Committee of Supply (COS), I spoke about Alibaba founder, Jack Ma, and his partner's intent to start the YunGu School – a 15-year through train system up to high school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I do not believe my reference was acknowledged or addressed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I had been stalking the online media of YunGu School and it has been inspiring so far – with a strong values base and a good balance in information technology (IT), other Science, Technology, Engineering, Art and Mathematics (STEAM) subjects.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have great confidence that Singapore can design an even more superior localised model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Do we dare pilot a through-train school of the future and, if good enough, scale it?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Past designers of the Singapore education system have often prided themselves in taking an evolutionary instead of a revolutionary approach.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But in a time such as this, we must have the dare to go beyond tweaking our school system or we will end up taking one step forward and two steps backward in preparing an education model that befits the future.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, the future of our children depends on what we are willing to do for education today.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We want to prepare our students to lead productive and successful lives once they leave the education system and enter the realm of working life.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the rapid changes around us, we may not know exactly what lies ahead for our students in the future and, at best, we can only try to ascertain what skillsets they might need by looking at current trends.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our graduating students must compete in an increasingly borderless world for the best jobs and, hence, they will need to be nimble, flexible and dynamic and ready to recognise and respond swiftly to emerging trends that call for new solutions, many of which moved into attempts into technological innovation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The students of today are adept at incorporating new technologies into their lives.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that we should tap into these new inclinations of our students and imbibe skills which would continue to make our labour force competitive to employers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, there is much to admire about the Singapore education system.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Yet, it is just as common to hear dissatisfaction from many quarters about this supposedly high-achieving education system of producing stressed-out, book-smart and exam-focused students who can do with more creativity, life skills, critical thinking and interpersonal skills.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Parents often feel trapped, together with their kids, in a desperate six-year race to safeguard their children's destinies by the tender age of 12.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The question is, what more needs to be done to keep Singapore ahead of the game in a new era of global talent?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The successful reinvention of our educational system depends on transforming pedagogy and redesigning learning tasks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can we spend less time in high-stakes exam preparations and more time in the joy of learning?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can we spend less time memorising facts and concepts and more time applying these to solve real-life problems?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can we nurture creative thinking, manage complex problems through collaboration and expose our students to a diversity of cultures, languages and practices in order to prepare them to be truly global citizens?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I believe our education system may prove to be Singapore's greatest strategic asset.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are blessed with highly-engaged parents, well-trained educators and generously-funded education institutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are well-poised to take the lead and make the necessary transformations to position Singaporeans strongly in the new economy, by making education a key pillar of our economic transformation efforts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, there are much needed and significant moves in the preschool sector which have placed greater importance on quality early childhood education for our children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With these moves, there is also a need to raise the quality of early childhood educators.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While NIEC will help to set benchmarks for standards of teaching and learning in the early childhood sector, early childhood educators must also be convinced that their professions are valued.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, career pathways need to be made clear and attainable for early childhood educators who seek to pursue preschool teaching as a career.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, sufficient recognition, rewards and incentives must also be made available for preschool educators, similar to how such recognition, rewards and incentives are available to mainstream primary and secondary school teachers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, there ought to be opportunities for preschool educators to be seconded to lower primary school levels, such as Primary 1 and 2, and vice versa.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We could probably pilot this with our MK teachers first.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This experience will help both our preschool and lower primary school educators better understand the transition required of our students as they progress from preschool to primary school.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will facilitate the planning of programmes as well as teaching and learning strategies at both the preschool and lower primary school levels that can help make the transition easier for our children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On top of that, it will also help our educators identify children who may be facing learning challenges to be identified earlier and proper intervention can then be rendered.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also propose for NIEC to consider running programmes that can equip stay-at-home mothers or fathers and grandparents or retirees with the requisite knowledge and skills to be caregivers to young children, whether to fulfil familial responsibilities or as a career option.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sufficient support and a conducive learning environment at home are equally important in providing quality early childhood education and development for our children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we strive to close the gaps in the provision of early childhood education in our preschools, we also need to help parents and grandparents create the same supportive and conducive environment at home for our children that can facilitate their learning and growth.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the stay-at-home mothers or fathers and retirees who are trained as caregivers to young children, they can also be considered as teaching assistants or edu-carers in our MKs or other preschool centres to support our preschool educators.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Recently, my friend from the corporate sector attended a kick-off meeting, where staff was introduced to the concept of VUCA, which stands for Volatile, Uncertain, Complex and Ambiguous, and the importance for both staff and organisation to be aware of and thrive in a VUCA environment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Similarly, in 2013, the then-Minister for Education envisaged what every Singapore child should achieve in 10 years of basic education, where deliberate shifts are made away from academic grades towards providing opportunities for students through diverse and real-world learning experiences to discover their interests and talents, develop life skills and find joy in learning because if the real world when they grow up is going to get more VUCA, then all the rigours in academia will not save them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am sure this number would be even higher now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I wish to ask the Minister to, firstly, provide an update on the Ministry's efforts to set students on a holistic learning trajectory, and how they are bearing fruit, as a midpoint check; secondly, review tuition cost expenditures, which disadvantage and pressurise students of lower socioeconomic backgrounds; and finally, take the lead and provide solid data that there is no link between tuition and better performance, to dispel the herd mentality of many parents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many Members have proposed and suggested measures and steps to be taken to achieve these two objectives.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of the most effective ways to do so is through our education system.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Psychology, in its broadest term, is the study of the human mind and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It has many disciplines, like personality, cognitive behaviour, social perception, to name some.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Individuals who have acquired a knowledge of psychology will most likely be able to recognise their own strengths and weaknesses and also of those people around them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: By knowing personal strengths and weaknesses, individuals will be better equipped to work on maximising their potential, and this will result in boosted self-esteem and confidence.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Naturally, the persons who are motivated will be the ones who try to innovate and think out of the box.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Being aware of others through the learning of psychology will contribute positively towards our ongoing effort in developing a more caring and gracious society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A person who is aware of the existence of different personalities and perspectives will be able to better apply acceptance and tolerance and respect these differences.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These are very important values to embrace in making our society more caring and gracious.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, from my recent exchange with the hon Senior Minister of State Dr Janil Puthucheary on Members of Parliament (MPs) speaking in schools, and from information subsequently obtained, I am not 100% sure, but it would seem that Government officeholders and grassroots advisers (GRAs) can go into MOE schools to officiate at events, hold dialogues on national issues and interact with students.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Senior Minister of State did not confirm this directly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That exchange was headlined in some media outlets as if I was advocating partisan politics in schools whereas the Government wants to keep politics out of schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I am arguing for is that we should balance up the exposure that students already have to People's Action Party (PAP) MPs wearing their GRA or Ministerial hats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The key phrase in what I said is "both sides".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not an adequate response to this to say that students can access views on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Exposing students to only one set of views from speakers in schools is unhealthy for the development of their critical faculties and their ability to see both sides of an issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should be able to pose questions and dialogue with elected public figures, both PAP and non-PAP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MPs from all parties play a role in our legislative process that is enshrined in the Constitution which our students study in schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Students should have the opportunity to hear directly from non-PAP Members of this House about their experience on the role they play in the national institution of Parliament and in the legislative work it undertakes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, it cannot be argued that Ministers and GRAs are, by definition, non-political when they talk to students, but non-PAP MPs are, by definition, political.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that non-PAP MPs can go into schools in their personal professional capacity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in that capacity, they cannot have dialogues about their role in the legislative process, whereas it would seem that PAP MPs can, wearing their Ministerial or GRA hats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that in the past, MPs could go into schools in their MP capacity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are public references online to MPs having officiated at school events in the past as MPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am told that there are many plaques in schools recording that a certain MP opened a particular school facility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In former PAP MP Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee's memoirs, he writes on page 18, and I quote, "I have made this call on many of the schools I spoke at during those early years as MP".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I noted that on at least two schools' websites that prior to 2011 or thereabouts schools would acknowledge MPs but, after that, the schools referred only to Grassroots Advisers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, we can pin labels that say "PAP is by definition okay"; "non-PAP is by definition partisan and hence not".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But does that serve the best interest of our students who will become the citizens of tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not make this a conversation about labels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us make this a conversation about what is best for our students.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, you can take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I applaud getting students to volunteer in a community through the Values in Action Programmes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many schools send their students overseas to do volunteer work and it is an eye-opener for many students when they visit the villages of neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, could schools also explore with voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) in the school vicinity so as to directly serve their community?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Schools could work with grassroots organisations to identify problems in the community and help to solve them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope MOE could dedicate more resources in this respect.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many students cringe when they attend National Education (NE) classes which could be known as different names in different schools but have similar results.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The only good thing, in the eyes of the students, is that there is no examination.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, it is important that our students appreciate the sweat, blood and hardship of our Pioneers in the early days of nation-building and understand and feel proud of how Singapore has transformed from Third-World to First.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some schools have tried to make NE more interesting.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, Evergreen Secondary School has just been given facilities for NE sharing and teaching, including an NE learning centre, political leadership corridors, movers and shakers' gallery.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Students can follow any trail by downloading an app.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: And this is an example of a school-based effort.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But how do we, as a whole, make any class more interesting and relevant?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, MOE could consider using contemporary issues to reflect the reality, constraints and limitations of being a small country.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Another possibility is to create milestone experiences where youths can feel proud to be a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, we could have activities to celebrate the issuing of the pink identity card (IC) to our 15-year-olds.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our mother tongue languages (MTLs) form the links to our cultural heritage and are the vehicle for the transmission of our cherished traditions and values.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Proficiency in our MTLs helps us to appreciate the richness of our culture and allows us to connect with our roots.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition to the recognition and reinforcement of our own identity, our MTLs are invaluable as a glue that gels our communities and enables us to communicate and connect with our counterparts around the region and other parts of the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For Singapore to continue to embrace this diversity as a strength in our multilingual and multicultural city, a strong command of our MTLs would be critical in helping our students to thrive in a rapidly changing global society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How will MOE engage our students and community to make the learning of our MTL come alive?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What are the steps that MOE will take to ensure that our students develop a deep appreciation and love of our MTLs not just in school, but also outside of school and beyond their schooling years?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Many Members have spoken of the importance of our region to our future.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Actually, our region is not only important to our future, but also to our past, to our sense of who we are and where we are rooted in the world.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Can we take the opportunity to complement these efforts in economic development with an increased focus in our school curriculum on teaching Bahasa Melayu?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is our National Language and a regional language.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I know our children who do not otherwise learn Malay have a lot to do already in school, including learning English, Chinese or Tamil to ever higher levels of proficiency.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Many Members have spoken of the importance of that, and they are right.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I believe it would be to the good if all our children could learn it to some basic level of conversational fluency.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Such learning will be good for the cognitive and intellectual development of our children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, with the backdrop of the rapidly disruptive economy and employment market, I am concerned that this special population would still be left behind unless we put in more strategic focus and priority.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But advances like artificial intelligence (AI) will not only replace low-skilled jobs but also some tasks performed in higher-skilled jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: How can MOE ensure that persons with special needs can continue to learn and upgrade their academic, vocational and life skills throughout their lives?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Recently, I was told of the story of Mary, and this is about enhanced support for those in mainstream schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I was told the story of Mary, not her real name, who is now 17 years old.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Her mother wrote, "We discovered Mary was musical from Primary 3.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: She was in the school choir and competed in international choir competitions, winning awards with the school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Also, a strong member of the speech and drama group.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: She was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and struggled in school with inconsistent learning support for her education needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: From the Express stream, she switched to the Normal Academic (NA) and, finding difficulty coping socially, she then also developed clinical depression.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Despite that, she pressed on with the family, spent much less time in music, passed her GCE N(A) examinations and scored an aggregate of 14 ‒ not good enough to qualify for LaSalle or NAFA because she did not have a GCE "O" level certificate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Mary is now in the ITE’s DPP Electrical Engineering programme for eligible GCE "N" level students because the programme does not have options in performing or creative arts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: She will spend the next two years in an engineering course of no interest to her, in the hope that she can get a NITEC certification in two years so that she can apply for LaSalle or NAFA." Sir, her mother wrote to me, not to complain, but to share to ask if better support could have been given to students with diverse needs and talents like Mary, and if there are other better options for young people like her.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: A highly-talented visually-impaired young pianist and composer, Adelyn, also faced the same dilemma.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The stricter Mother Tongue exemption policy in mainstream schools, too, has impacted students with diverse needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: A respected psychologist consultant in the private sector who consults for the MOE actually is in grief when countless appeals that he made to exempt his child from Mother Tongue were rejected unless she fails in all subjects.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This is notwithstanding the fact that she is diagnosed to have dyspraxia and other learning challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Learning is a big struggle and the family is waiting for the 12 years of compulsory education to be over and is seriously contemplating other options for their life after Primary 6.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But what of others who are not able to afford other options?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: On Special Education (SPED) schools, I am very thankful to Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary who chaired the Compulsory Education (CE) Committee and good work has been done to understand the needs and also to obtain suggestions from many focus groups, comprising students, staff and families.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Many issues were raised that relate to how the quality of SPED schools can be further enhanced so that the stigma could be removed and every SPED school is and perceived as a school of choice for students who are better off in this specialist setting.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They have potential and can contribute to society, if given a fair chance and the appropriate training and support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They say, it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But it takes a leader to lead the village.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For a first-world education system, MOE must lead and assemble the right helping hands and take its place to facilitate stronger support for learners with diverse and special needs in our country.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I welcome the decision in Budget 2018 to increase support for education.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Indeed, every Singaporean should have access to quality education, regardless of their background.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another teacher said that she has three special needs kids out of 24 in her preschool class.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It would be good if preschools which are willing to take in kids with special needs can have additional funding and training.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can we expect future enhancements to existing schemes and also for these programmes to be available in MKs, if there is not any now?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Is it time to work out something so that some of these children can have a seamless transition from preschool to primary as well?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I understand that MOE has been retooling the education system to shift the unhealthy focus on academic competition to emphasise holistic education and the love of learning.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But a culture of "academic results focus" has already set in among the parents.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We cannot blame the parents because they want to give the best to their children.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: They learned the culture from the old focus on academic competition, believing in the old paradigm of good grades and a linear path from elite primary schools to the top universities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: When they are faced with globalisation and technological disruptions, they become even more anxious about making sure their children get the best start in life.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: MOE should not stop to complete the transformation of the system despite these diehard habits.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It will take time to change such an entrenched culture.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, MOE could also look into communicating and educating parents on the many pathways to success in the new economy, so as to lessen their anxiety and, thus, lessen the transfer of the anxiety to their children.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, there are a few fundamental tenets of a child's education which I believe most of us, if not all, will subscribe to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, always be prepared to try something new ‒ push the envelope, break new ground, do something we have never done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Who knows, it might turn out that you will enjoy the new adventure, arise to a fresh challenge?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Being always or even often successful is no good to a young child.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Learn to lose and be gracious in defeat.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Pick up, dust off, try again, be stronger and better the next time round.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Third, we have to work as a team.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: No man is an island, and no one functions in silos.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Our children have to be able to work and play with one another and to support, complement, encourage and cheer one another on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They have to learn to come together to make a cohesive team, a team which would be stronger than the sum of its parts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It takes a lot of hard work to become good at anything, and even more hard work to remain good and stay ahead of the competition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These are all simple basic values, but the foundation and cornerstone for bringing up the women and men of tomorrow, the leaders of our next generation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I believe, Sir, that all of these are best taught, not in the classroom, but on the playing field.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And I am quite sure most in this House would, I hope, agree with that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Very often, a child's first encounter with sports, especially team sports, would be in school when they first enrolled for their primary education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Schools, therefore, play a crucial role in being the first mover in introducing sports into our children's lives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And should there be sufficient interest and sufficient talent demonstrated, the school invariably would also take the additional active role of identifying and eventually nurturing that talent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Sports, therefore, offer an educational platform for our children which cannot be easily replicated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: On that score, I would like to raise a few queries and have some suggestions for the Minister's consideration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is important because not every child can afford or have an opportunity to be exposed to sports outside of school.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: How is anyone going to know if he or she can be good at sports if they have no opportunity to try that sport?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, the initial formative years in their primary school would be crucial.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For instance, not offering, say, hockey or badminton as a school co-curricular activity (CCA) option would quite likely mean that the child might never be exposed to that sport.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This, in turn, then limits the selection base from which a young budding talent might be identified and, in turn, then subsequently limits the base from which national athletes could be selected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: From a resourcing perspective, I understand that it would, of course, not be possible for every school to offer every sport.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But could more be done to enhance the range of options available?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Alternatively, is MOE working with Sport SG or Active SG in promoting sporting options to our school children and make sports more accessible?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The MOE website indicates that students who are keen on an activity which may not be offered by the school could seek the school's approval to set up that activity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: How often has this been done and, in any event, is it realistic?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, there has been some public discussions about mealtimes as more schools move to single sessions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parents are concerned that the children are eating late lunches in the mid-afternoon and not having enough time to eat snacks during recess time due to the scheduling of classes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While nutritionists say that there are no set hours for children to have their meals, they also advise that children should have three main meals and two to three snacks at regular hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that MOE leaves it to the schools to decide on their daily schedules.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, Sir, inflation is an inevitable and intractable global issue.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am concerned about the rising living costs, how they will impact our students from low socioeconomic families.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In spite of the subsidies, bursaries, scholarships and grants, there are some students who will still fall through the cracks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The distractions of part-time work and social problems at home may prevent them from focusing on their studies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This results in a vicious cycle where the poor cannot do well in school and they are unable to break out of the poverty cycle.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How are they given equal access to opportunities for all students regardless of their family and income backgrounds?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Chairman, Sir, the Edusave awards and bursaries scheme has provided an excellent opportunity to our students to incentivise them, motivate them and give them a platform on which they can celebrate their achievements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The extension of the Edusave awards to non-academic achievements has also been very well-received.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The news that this already very popular scheme has been given additional resourcing, particularly targeted for the lower- to middle-income, has been very well-received.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The programme has proven useful not only to defray some of the costs of education for the family but also provides an opportunity for students to use this to tap on school-based enrichment programmes to enhance holistic learning beyond the boundaries of the classroom or the textbook.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Can the Minister please elaborate further on what enrichment options there might be?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE is committed to giving every child the best start in life – not just in school, but for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Denise Phua, Mr Seah Kian Peng, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Zainal Sapari highlighted the driving trends of today and asked how we will prepare our children for the future economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I agree with them that given the trends, tomorrow's jobs will require innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will prepare our children from young and we start from a position of strength.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Over the years, we have developed an education system that is effective in inculcating students with sound values and equipping them with a strong academic foundation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have built upon this base in the last few years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One, we have strengthened our focus on the holistic development of every child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have dialled back from an over-emphasis on academic grades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Teachers today coordinate to manage the assessment and homework load.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We took steps to reduce the competitive pressures in our system, so that students can focus on their learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked if we can pilot no-PSLE through-train schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I understand her good intentions, as well as the stresses that parents and students face.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Stress arises from a complex mix of factors – policies, expectations, perceptions, mindsets and ground realities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The PSLE changes we have made are important changes at the policy level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This guides the child to a suitable academic programme in secondary school, one that would best fit his learning needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: PSLE does not, however, cast in stone what students can achieve in school in life or anytime in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The anxieties at Primary 1 then would be tremendous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Also, the GCE "O" and "N" levels at the end of this through-train will really be most stressful.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A single examination in the whole career of a child's life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Faisal Manap suggested for MOE to introduce psychology in the secondary school curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Psychology, however, is an abstract discipline, not an age-appropriate subject at secondary school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A better broader approach to fulfil the same intent is to focus on 21st century competencies in our curriculum, create more space for informal learning, learning through play, and encourage opportunities for character building in the classroom, outside the classroom, in the CCAs, including our enhanced Outdoor Education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These support the socio-emotional development in our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked about the 21st century Competencies Framework and when it was last reviewed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It was last reviewed in 2014 and also during the time when I entered MOE when I took a fresh look at the Framework.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our teachers in tandem are provided many professional development opportunities and resources to support their learning and keep them updated on all the different "gogies" that Ms Denise Phua has mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have also initiated the Singapore Teaching Practice where the best teaching practices are shared online amongst teachers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Beyond academic strengths and interests, we are providing many opportunities for discovery and talent development in the sports and the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Edwin Tong made good points about sports in schools and developing sporting talent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, primary school students learn fundamental movement skills in different sports in their Physical Education (PE) lessons, a wide range.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Primary 4 and 5 students who are interested in sports CCAs not offered by the school can consider joining MOE’s centrally-run Junior Sports Academies, which offer a variety of sports modules.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In secondary school, students learn at least six sports and take part in at least three inter-class sports competitions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A third of our students enroll in sports CCAs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our schools understand that the value of sports cannot be measured by performance merely in the inter-school games.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE also promotes programmes organised by ActiveSG to encourage our students when they are not in school to participate in sports in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Three, we are developing positive attitudes and dispositions for lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I have highlighted repeatedly in this House and outside, the need to nurture the joy of learning and entrepreneurial dare.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These are important because they sustain self-directed, lifelong learning and instill an innovative, entrepreneurial spirit in our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These may not be measurable but are certainly observable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They are of utmost importance to shift us away from simply studying for exams to learning for life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The many changes I have mentioned are meant to take pressure off parents and students, reducing the chasing after the last mark in our school system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ultimately, I hope to partner parents and students themselves to reduce their anxieties and stress.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many parents I have spoken to tell me they agree with the directions that we have taken.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They also asked, like Ms Foo Mee Har, what will all these mean for their children’s learning experiences in school?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As I mentioned earlier, our education system today equips our students with a strong academic foundation and sound values.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Pritam Singh mentioned education systems in Israel and Finland in the Budget Debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Indeed, there are strengths in these systems which we can learn from.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But we are circumspect when we study other systems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We do not blindly seek to replicate other systems in Singapore nor simply adopt new trends.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In fact, these countries are also looking towards Singapore and wanting to learn from us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Consider Israel: I visited Israel and looked at their talent development and innovation ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It has a strong disposition in this area but, overall, it has big averages.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There is also a significant education outcomes gap between the average and the top Israeli students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Rather, we will improve our education system by building on our existing strengths, even as we explore new possibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Let us not throw out the baby with the bath water.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As such, on top of strong academic foundations and sound values, we want to get our students to move beyond the classroom and apply their knowledge in the real world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will help nurture our next generation of "change-makers".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our students must be able to connect their "Head" knowledge to their "Hands" and create value.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And their "Hands" must also be connected to their "Hearts" so that they contribute their knowledge and skills to the betterment of society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Education must go beyond the classroom and academic grades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I will focus the rest of my speech on how we will anchor this within our education system, through the lived experiences of our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But, first, let me tell Members a "Story of Two Cars".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I met two 10-year-old boys at a community event some time ago.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They wanted to show me their toy car.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I thought to myself initially what was this about?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But when I saw the car, I got interested.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: You see, the car was not any sexy toy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It was very plain, made up of cardboard.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The boys took some of their mother's shoe boxes, cut off the top and bottom and fashioned a flat chassis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They then got a set of wheels, mounted them on together with some rudimentary drive train and wired the system up.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Then, they applied what they had learnt about energy in their Science class.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They put on top of the chassis miniature solar panels and made their own solar-powered car.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Their eyes sparkled when they talked to me on that Saturday morning as they showed me their solar toy car.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This car is made out of pure fun, pure curiosity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These boys, all of 10 years old, applied what they had learnt in Science class to build their own toy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The second car is also a solar-powered car but, this time, it is a racing car.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This car was built by a team of Singapore Polytechnic students taking part in the 2017 World Solar Challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They competed against 39 other teams from all over the world, including Cambridge University and Stanford University.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They took 20 months to make that car using a high-tech carbon fibre-reinforced composite body.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The top speed of this solar car is 100 kilometres per hour (km/h), built by 18- to 20-year-old boys.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They met with rough weather, an accident and, unfortunately, did not finish within the deadline.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, I want to celebrate their success and include them in my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This car was built out of passion, deep skills and resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Though they may not have won, the learning in their journey is invaluable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These two cars may be miles apart in technology and horsepower but, educationally, they are part of the same journey – from curiosity to mastery; from knowledge to application.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want all our students to be able to make this type of learning journey.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is a mode of learning for all students, not just a separate track for vocational students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They see for themselves how they can apply what they have learnt to the real world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And from all the interactions I had with students, I see them enjoying learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: All the ALPs, importantly, encourage exploration, ideation and creativity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students learn through experimentation – they try, fail, try, learn from it and try again.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I recently met some Fuchun secondary students and they tell me their school has an ALP called "Innovations in Science and Technology for Sustainability".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They all learnt basic coding and programming and apply their coding skills to programme robots.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Together with his team, Zee Cheen designed and built from scratch a robot that could move on different terrains, even on water, to retrieve and transport objects.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Zee Cheen told me that when they started, and I quote, "Everything was in a mess." They had to learn to work as a team, put in place a plan, work each bolt, gear and wire step-by-step to fulfil their design.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Surprisingly, Zee Cheen told me that his biggest lesson through this ALP was not just in creating the robot.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: His team has to bring their robot to the Science Centre's Maker Faire.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And he had to practise public speaking and he says it is not his forte.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He had to explain his robot to each visitor interested in his robot!

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In his words, he said, "These are things I cannot learn in a classroom".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the value of applied learning in real life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some of our primary schools have also developed ALPs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I have visited Teck Whye Primary which runs an ALP called "Media Whiz Kids!" I met Maisarah, a cute petite Primary 5 student.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She wanted to help her schoolmates tell fake news apart from real news.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, she worked with her friends and teachers to make a short three-minute video.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the video, Maisarah explains what fake news is, why people create it, and she also suggests how to tackle it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We all debate about fake news in this very Chamber.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through Applied Learning Programmes, our 10-year-old students are teaching it in their own way in school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is a refreshing take on a very real concern.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Maisarah and her friends narrate and present with great confidence and clarity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Importantly, Maisarah's teachers not only use the video to raise information literacy among their students but also inculcate values.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The video has been uploaded onto the school's Facebook and I encourage all of us to take a look.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am very proud of the confident and creative students our schools have nurtured through ALPs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But I am even prouder of our teachers, who have committed their time and effort to develop Applied Learning experiences for their students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Elaine Koh, a teacher I met from Fuchun Secondary, told me the difference she saw in her Secondary 4 Normal (Technical) students, Viknesh and Kumaran, after they have participated in the Maker Faire.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She shared that they were very engaged and focused when they tinkered and built things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And when I met Viknesh and Kumaran, they told me they are interested to study aeronautical and mechanical engineering at ITE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They want to design and build aeroplanes and racing cars.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: ALP has ignited a passion in them, to want to continue their learning and their maker journey.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: ALPs are intentional ways to spur innovation in our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will also support schools with ALPs to further enhance and strengthen their capabilities and programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is an investment worth making – nurture innovation and creativity and, importantly, prepare our children for our future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And I will remember to add, the artistic element into it as well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is not just in the applied fields where Applied Learning is relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our teachers are making a big effort to infuse Applied Learning experiences into their day-to-day teaching.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, we are using Applied Learning to make our MTLs come alive for our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will help foster their appreciation for languages and strengthen their proficiency, which Ms Tin Pei Ling spoke about, and which Mr Azmoon Ahmad and Mr Low Thia Khiang also mentioned in the Budget Debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In Mandarin):   Although our education system is well-regarded by the international community, many people are still concerned that in a future where automation is the norm, will our next generation be replaced by machines?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But I am confident that as long as our education system can empower our children to be creative and acquire good values, our next generation will be able to grasp the opportunities in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In order to cultivate creativity from young, MOE is now promoting Applied Learning in our schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our students already have a solid academic foundation; but we do not want them to be only able to "talk about strategies on paper" and become nerds who only know how to talk but not how to do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They must know how to convert knowledge into power and use it in real life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Only by applying intelligently what you have learnt can you create infinite possibilities with finite knowledge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students of Yuan Qing Secondary School are learning to write xinyao (新谣) in the Chinese classes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through song writing, their language ability will improve and they can also appreciate the beauty of the language better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One student, Guo Zifeng, wrote a song, "My Mother".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The lyrics are very touching and the melody beautiful, expressing his love and gratitude to his mother.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The song won an award in the 2017 Xinyao Singing and Writing Competition.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The work of Zifeng makes us understand the importance of right values.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However good a person’s knowledge base and creative capability may be, if his values are flawed, he will bring greater harm to society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, we introduced various programmes in our schools to instill good values in our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We teach them to be centred on the right morals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This has been our education principle all along.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Applied learning should not be confined to a particular subject and the classroom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We hope parents can do the same in daily life to give our children more space and time for applied learning and instill right values in them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Parents can work together with the school and create a better future for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In English): I will now move on to connecting the "Hands" and the "Heart".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is critical that we equip our children with the right values and develop in them a heart for others.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Without the right moral compass, talented individuals can do more harm to society than good, and that will be tragic.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Just like knowledge, values cannot remain simply in the "head".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They must be acted out, applied to the real world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng encouraged schools and students to work with their local communities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I mentioned my visit to Teck Whye Primary earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: During my visit, I met a Primary 6 student.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She showed me a pair of chopsticks that she and her team designed for people with weaker muscular control, such as our elderly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Zer Jynn explained that she and her team had first thought of a catch-and-release mechanism to allow users to use the chopsticks with minimal strength.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And she built this model, nothing fancy, using simple materials – chopsticks, a straw, a spring and a masking tape.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And in this model, she designed something to help the elderly grab food.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She experimented several times until she was satisfied with the catch-and-release function.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With this design, she went on to 3D-print a plastic prototype, with the help of her teachers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, she is not satisfied with the plastic prototype as it did not work as well as her initial prototype.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: You see, she has probably reversed the hinge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But I have given her some possibilities and she told me she will work to improve her prototype.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Her schoolmates in the Teck Whye Primary iDesign Club have built learning aids for their peers with dyslexia, and other prototypes to improve the quality of life for the physically disabled or the elderly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through the iDesign Club, they not only learn about design principles but, equally important, they are tacitly learning to care, empathise and serve others in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Zer Jynn and her schoolmates may only be in primary school but, under the guidance of their school and teachers, they exemplify what we want to nurture in our young the connection among the head, the heart and the hands, innovating to improve the lives of others, developing leadership, empathy, care and, importantly, resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Applied learning in real life is so much more effective than just doing it in the classroom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Besides developing solutions for the community, our schools and students have also partnered the community to strengthen culture and heritage.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A good example is Bulan Bahasa – the Malay Language Month.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The community hosts activities, such as writing workshops and storytelling, that broaden students' exposure to language and culture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They set up activity booths for the public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They also take on the roles of Rakan Bahasa, or Friends of the Language, to serve as museum guides at the Malay Heritage Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The two-way partnership between schools and community not only enhances the learning of students but allows them to put values into action and serve the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In a separate event at Fiesta Bahasa, this time round at the National Library, I was very happy to see a batch of Hwa Chong Institution boys participating.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: You see, they were learning Malay, trying to learn to speak it fluently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These Chinese boys from a Special Assistance Plan (SAP) school were interacting with our Malay students and parents naturally, without a hint of any language barrier!

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, this is applied learning in action, in languages, to promote our Singapore's unique cultures and heritage.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As we strive to build a caring and inclusive society, we must make sure no child is left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This included upgrading the preschool profession to attract good teachers and careers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Most faculty are experienced practitioners in the preschool sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Separately, MOE has facilitated professional exchanges between MK educators and also primary school teachers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They help develop mutual understanding, which smoothens the transition from kindergarten to Primary 1.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: SLS will provide high-quality, curriculum-aligned learning resources and online learning tools for students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will drive self-directed learning which can take place anytime, anywhere and, hopefully, reduce the reliance contribution as well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE has provided funding to schools, which can be used to subsidise students from less advantaged backgrounds, for them to purchase mobile learning devices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With this increase, students can participate in more activities, such as creative writing programmes and learning journeys, to broaden their learning experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government also provides a range of financial assistance schemes to assist those who are in need.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Cheng Li Hui asked about this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the primary to pre-university levels, Singaporean students who need assistance can tap on the MOE FAS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is in answer to Assoc Prof Daniel Goh.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will also increase the income eligibility criteria for the Edusave Merit Bursary and Independent School Bursary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, I have said what MOE, our schools and teachers are committed to doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But let me emphasise that we cannot do this alone.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need the whole nation to move with us towards holistic education, and parents play a most important role.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I strongly urge all parents to give our children the time for their minds to imagine; space for them to experiment and learn to embrace and take risks; opportunities to learn from failing, trying, relearning and trying until they succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, let me conclude with a story.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I visited Assumption English School last July to open their upgraded school site.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The opening ceremony was a most unusual one, hinged on robots programmed by their students part of an ALP.
