speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I was invited to participate in a robot race on stage, to move the robots, in order to switch on a ray of bright-coloured lights to mark the official opening of the school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The robots were powered solely by wind and controlled by an iPad.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: My engineering mind straightaway went into a thinking mode and I thought these robots could fail easily and, when they fail to function, the bulbs will not light up, and the failure will be significant, in front of the whole school, a hall full of parents, students, MOE senior officials.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: After the ceremony, I congratulated the then principal, Mrs Mabel Leong, and I quietly asked her "What would you have done if the robots did not work?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What was the backup?" She told me quietly, too, "Minister, there is no back up." She said that if the robots did not work despite all their planning and efforts, she would have simply stood up, apologised to me and sought my understanding to skip the segment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In spite of the risks, she decided to keep the robot segment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I suspect because she is proud of her students and it showcased her students' pride in their learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I must tell you, I smiled the widest smile in an entire week, knowing what Mable was doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our principals and schools are moving in the right direction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: More of them are taking calculated risks for their students to have the time and space for experimentation, to try, fail, try again, even in front of a Minister!

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Seeing how the schools and educators are changing, I sincerely urge all parents to join us in creating similar opportunities for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The results of such opportunities may not be immediately apparent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But the true test for all of us is not any single examination.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is such opportunities that will benefit our children for a lifetime, much more than cramping their free time with excessive tuition.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I hope all parents will encourage their children when they participate in their schools' ALPs, Outdoor Education Programme, Values-in-Action activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Engage them in conversation over their Applied Learning experiences, share in their successes and setbacks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Share in their joys, empathise with their failings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Create more of such learning experiences for them in the classroom and outside the classroom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With the full support from educators and, most importantly, parents, our children will get the best start in life, whatever the future may bring.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will acquire the skills and values to thrive in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A brighter future of greater fulfilment awaits them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To prepare each of our students for the future, MOE has to be prepared to do different things, and to do things differently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some of this expertise did not traditionally reside with MOE.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We partnered VWOs which had deep expertise in SEN support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And as both sides learnt from each other, these partnerships evolved to strengthen support for our students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One good example of this is our relationship with AWWA, with whom we work on different service models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The partnership extends to mainstream schools, where Asian Women Welfare Association (AWWA) provides training and consultation services to our educators, supporting students with physical and visual impairments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I say that again to make sure we are all clear – 80% of our students with SEN are enrolled in mainstream schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They are supported not just by allied educators, but also by educational psychologists and suitable intervention programmes, including those provided by organisations, such as AWWA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As our students move on to the post-secondary space, they are supported by SEN Support Offices in each of our IHLs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are also looking ahead and constantly seeking ways to better support our students to realise their potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are different ways to do this, including the suggestion of an academy for those with special needs and all who support them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are enhancing the professional development for our staff and are also looking at how to better support students with SEN at key transition points, like when they enter schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Strong partnership between MOE and the community has also enabled the sector to make significant improvements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over the past year, MOE has worked with our Government-funded SPED schools to ensure the smooth implementation of compulsory education for children with moderate to severe special needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are confident that students who can benefit from such specialised support will receive quality education in these schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Yet, as Ms Denise Phua has pointed out, our efforts must go beyond legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE and our partners must continue to look for ways to do better, to deliver affordable, quality Specialised Education for our students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Grace Orchard School, an early participant of the School-to-Work Transition Programme (S2W) did several new things to ensure that their students benefited from the opportunity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They reached out to the private sector for job opportunities; they updated their curriculum, so that the students could start their job training in their last years within the school.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are also looking into lifelong learning opportunities for those with special needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our SkillsFuture Credit course directory is continually updated with new courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also have a SkillsFuture Study Award for Persons with Disabilities to recognise those who demonstrate resilience and perseverance in pursuing lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I can address a few of the specific queries that Miss Cheng Li Hui and Ms Denise Phua brought up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The DSP programme, together with EIPIC, is organised by MSF and I need to defer to them to talk about those interventions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But there are three MKs that offer the DSP programme and we will study how we can do that better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To Ms Denise Phua's questions, all teachers since 2005 have been equipped with SEN training during their pre-service training at the National Institute of Education (NIE).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Each school also has a group of teachers who have undergone certificate level training in special needs at NIE.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are known teachers trained in special needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about National Education (NE).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are people who feel that the storyline is worn and tired, or, as Mr Ang Wei Neng expressed it, that NE is propaganda.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our recommendations centre on nurturing a sense of belonging to our country and community, a sense of Singapore's realities and challenges, and a sense of shared hope and aspirations as a nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our efforts to refresh and improve NE will then be driven by three groups of interventions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: First, just as learning must evolve to remain relevant, NE discussions must take on contemporary issues, as well as the perspectives of different Singaporeans, including our students themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will enable our students' shared appreciation for the ever-evolving Singapore story.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about how we expose our students to diverse perspectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is already happening, is already done in subjects like Social Studies, History and Geography.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Students undertake learning journeys, they come to Parliament to visit and witness Parliamentary debates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our students examine evidence and different viewpoints before arriving at informed and reasoned conclusions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This includes exploring the rationale behind policy decisions, and the pros and cons of alternatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In General Paper (GP) lessons, students consider different perspectives and learn to differentiate between fact and opinion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Bendemeer Secondary School is a school which already makes a conscious effort to do so and provides an example of how we can develop the process further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When I visited the school, I saw students have lively discussions on their own on issues relevant to Singapore, such as the environment, a car-lite society, technology and future jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The school is looking to deepen this practice in their Character and Citizenship Education periods, so that students have the time and space to explore their convictions and reflect upon such issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our students may not always agree with one another, Indeed, in Bendeemer Secondary School, the session that I witnessed, there was a lively debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They may not even agree with their teachers, but we do want to ensure that there is space for respectful conversations and that we nurture in our students open-mindedness, respect for one another and that they develop the skills for critical thinking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The second group of interventions is that we will facilitate citizenship experiences which empower our students, allowing them to find their own meaning as citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are already milestone experiences throughout a student’s journey in our schools, such as the NE Show for all primary students, subsequently, things like the Outward Bound School.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Schools like Ping Yi Secondary School decided to try something different.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We look forward to making more of such cohort or school-based experiences meaningful and available for our students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, a third thrust of our efforts supports teachers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They have been doing well and, going forward, we will include more professional development opportunities and involve experienced educators in spearheading pedagogical innovation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If I may return to some of the questions that Mr Leon Perera asked, he took a particular view about labels and perhaps my labelling of his comments has partisan politics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Perhaps, I may need to expand upon why I believe that is an apt explanation for what he is asking for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Member himself has acknowledged that he has attended schools in a non-partisan, non-political capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is no obstruction to him doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What he is asking for, is for him to be allowed to attend in any partisan political capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He seems to believe that he has previously attended in a non-partisan political capacity, but I am assuming that the reason he is asking to attend in a partisan capacity, because he is assuming that everybody else attends only in a political partisan capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is a level of hubris that is really quite remarkable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If he can attend in a non-partisan, non-political way, I think the assumption should be, in good faith that other people can do as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What he is asking for, what he is implying, is for him to attend in a partisan political way somehow provides balance within our existing framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is not what we do currently, and so it would be inappropriate for an invitation to be extended to him in his capacity as a member of a political party and as an MP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is an explanation that what he is asking for is inappropriate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about our students' nutritional health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE had worked with the Health Promotion Board (HPB) to survey our students' nutritional habits, and also in the rollout of the Healthy Meals in Schools Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Under this programme, canteen stalls prepare food with healthier ingredients and use healthier cooking methods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our schools also recognise that students benefit from meal breaks so that they can sustain their energy and focus.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Students have two meal breaks a day, with a longer lunch break if there are afternoon programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also help our students understand the importance of a healthy and balanced diet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Primary school students are taught to read food labels, to plan healthy meals and the importance of eating enough and eating right.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As MOE and HPB continue to work to build up their knowledge and their habits, I must stress the vital role that parents play in reinforcing these healthy habits at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about MOE's tracking of social mobility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On MOE's part, we track closely the progress of all students in our education system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Like other countries, we do pay close attention to those from more disadvantaged family backgrounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We monitor how they fare in school, including at key milestones of education attainment, their progression to post-secondary institutions, including the polytechnics and universities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More importantly, we put in place programmes to give extra support to those who need it right from early childhood prior to Primary 1, and many different interventions, including meals, career counselling and learning support programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As a result of these interventions, we have made significant progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We start early on, we ensure access to quality education for all students and, on top of that, levelling-up programmes for the disadvantaged to give them every opportunity for success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With MKs and NIEC, we are also seeking to improve access to quality preschool education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our efforts to provide space for exploration and applied learning in schools will benefit all students, regardless of their background.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In the higher education space, as well as in our future economy, it is about the diversity of pathways that recognise and reward different strengths, as well as investments in continuous learning and relearning that will ultimately serve our mission of ensuring that social mobility is maintained in this nation of ours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What has remained unchanged is the belief that all of us together – MOE, schools, parents and the community – must continue to provide all our students with opportunities and experiences that bring out the best in them so that we can all realise our collective potential as a nation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I believe that it is important to help students be curious and engaged in what they are learning.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Such is what is needed to encourage lifelong learning, a necessary skill for success in the real world.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Aptitude-based admission presents another approach to evaluate the students' strengths and weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Such an awareness may allow the education system to equip them with the skills that are best suited for their abilities and interests.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Personally, I see aptitude-based evaluation as a means to uncover hidden gems amongst our students, ensuring that the education system is able to recognise these latent abilities and offer them the best possible chance for their career development.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Hence, can MOE share its plans to offer more courses based on Aptitude-Based Admission to our ITEs?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It gives hope and confidence to the students whose academic grades may otherwise be inadequate and inspires them to keep on pushing on with their dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The exemplary performance of students from the pioneer batch who have graduated last year is an indication of the success of this programme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Perhaps the polytechnics may wish to offer the option to other students who may have qualified for admission to polytechnic but need extra help.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Considering the overall performance of PFP's Pioneer Batch, I wish to ask what further plans does the Minister have to support the aspirations of the students who opt for this pathway.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: CEP would enable students to be exposed to different specialisations within engineering, before deciding on a specific engineering diploma.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I understand that these are for students who are interested to pursue this broad subject but would like more time to discover their areas of interests before selecting a diploma of their choice in the second semester or second year.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Many of us have been in that position before – not sure what to do, what we would like to do, what to pursue for our studies and for our career.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, I think having such a CEP is a good move.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: With this exposure, the students will have opportunities to tread on shallow water before taking the plunge, thus minimising bad career decisions at the end of the road.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It is also a way for us to embed the required DNA, core of the discipline into each subject, while giving students free rein to explore their specialisation later on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: At the broader level, can the Minister provide an update on its efforts to provide more options for polytechnic students to explore their interests and strengths before choosing their specific course of study?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I have two other specific questions for the Minister as follows: (a) are there now more engineering graduates with the inception of CEP; and (b) secondly, does the Minister intend to expand CEP to non-engineering subjects?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Chairman, in order to better prepare our students to be skilled and competent and to be able to hit the ground running when they enter the workforce, it is important that they receive hands-on training in skillsets which dovetail into and complement the industry sectors they are trained for.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This not only provides our industries with well-trained and upskilled employees but also gives the new trainees an opportunity to master the trade from an early stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this light, the Work-Learn Technical Diploma (WLTD) programme, which is about to commence shortly for ITE graduates, is very much to be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This programme provides graduates with first-hand experience to learn, practise and do at the same time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What has been the feedback so far from students' and participating employers?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And are there plans to grow the number of applicable industries and participating partnering employers?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, many ITE students and graduates are good with their hands and less brilliant in paper-and-pen examinations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Singapore is far behind some parts of the world in nurturing technical skills.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For example, in the UK, apprenticeship programmes offer work-based learning which can lead to a bachelor's or master's degree.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: These dual-training programmes are a mix of theory and hands-on training in areas like advanced Manufacturing, IT, Banking and Hospitality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In fact, they are paid for the time they take for the training.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As a result of this programme, the youth jobless rate in Germany is very low.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, like Mr Edwin Tong, I would like MOE to give an update on WLTD, as well as the Work-Study Degree programme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The rapid development of technology has benefited lives and also disrupted lives at the same time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Many skillsets learnt during an undergraduate course a decade ago can turn obsolete in just one year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Gone are the days where a graduate degree can last for life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: We need to relearn, retool, re-energise throughout our working lives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: What roles do our oldest public universities like the National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) play in promoting lifelong learning?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Are these IHLs adequately funded to provide courses for lifelong learning?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Currently, NUS has a School of Continuing and Lifelong Learning offering Bachelor of Technology programmes, specialised certificate courses and courses for Executives and Professionals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How do IHLs ensure the courses offered are relevant to emerging trends and future needs?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How are they working with industrial players to ensure that courses are useful and future-ready?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Since the launch of the SkillsFuture movement, there are numerous initiatives implemented to help Singaporeans upskill, reskill, deep-skill and cross-skill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Nonetheless, amidst the plethora of SkillsFuture offerings, how successful have we been in helping Singaporeans not just improve or expand their repertoire of skills, but also helping them remain employed or even become more employable?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How extensive are efforts to increase awareness amongst students and employees on the opportunities that SkillsFuture offers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How aware are Singaporeans about the various SkillsFuture courses that they have for them?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How extensively are our universities and IHLs working with employers to implement such SkillsFuture initiatives and programmes?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Probably, a separate category can be set up to help Singaporeans navigate MySkillsFuture or SkillsConnect portals and identify employers who are keen to support them in such SkillsFuture programmes, beyond just the usual job vacancies that employers have within their respective organisations.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: This will facilitate job searches by Singaporeans and help them identify employers who are supportive of skills training among their employees.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It would also be good to link employers to support SkillsFuture programmes with the educational institutions that provide such SkillsFuture programmes within these online platforms to make it easier for Singaporeans planning their career and training and development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Wealth Management Institute, a SkillsFuture training provider.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: It was driven by the imperative to have Singaporeans develop new capabilities for the future and embrace a culture of lifelong learning in order to ride the waves of change brought about by rapid technological disruptions and economic restructuring.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: It is unclear to me how successful we have been on this journey.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: For the movement to gather more traction with both employers and employees, there must be clear linkages between training courses to skills acquisition and improving career prospects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: We can be justifiably proud of the capabilities of public sector IHLs in producing graduates with strong employment prospects, as evidenced by employment surveys and low youth unemployment rates.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: But the ecosystem for continuing education and training is not endowed with the same scale, resources and infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: As more and more learning is expected to take place after one joins the workforce, adult learning will become an increasingly important part of our education system.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: We should really consider setting up a national institute of ICT for professionals to provide a comprehensive set of training programmes that facilitate aspiring professionals’ entry to the industry, while offering seasoned professionals skills for them to master and apply in this particularly attractive industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We are all familiar with PISA, and PIAAC stands for the Programme for International Assessment of Adult Competencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s inclusion in such studies would not have been possible without the Ministry's progressive efforts and support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By highlighting potential gaps in policy, the findings from such surveys are useful in guiding early intervention strategies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the information they provide can improve the efficiency with which intervention is applied.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s corresponding rankings for numeracy skills and reading skills are also high, at 6th and 7th respectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What this implies is that workers who have skills deficiencies could be expected to perform significantly poorer in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My interpretation of the results of the PIAAC survey is that the proportion of workers in Singapore who may be at risk of skills deficiency is not insignificant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: While the results of surveys must be looked at in perspective, the areas of concern they point to in Singapore’s case suggest that lack of basic literacy and ICT skills appears to affect skills performance in other areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This could imply those without foundation in literacy and ICT skills will not be able to make further progress in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This higher variance in skills proficiency suggests that training has to be much more carefully tailored to individual needs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government has increased its spending in education and lifelong learning in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's ageing population and declining birth rate will directly affect the structure of our workforce in the future.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the constraints of our small population, we have always championed the idea of everyone contributing towards one's best, and that everyone could get to use one's value and talent fully.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I fully support increasing our investments into education, and giving greater attention to raise the quality of our human resources so that our economy will continue to develop and prosper.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Trade associations are willing to play an active part in this long-term plan to develop human resources.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Our IHLs provide one of the key sources of business talents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The training and curriculum in IHLs should match the actual needs of the business community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, if trade associations could collaborate closely with IHLs to educate our students in accordance with the practical needs of the businesses, it would be an arrangement that produces many benefits.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: From what I know, in the aspect of curriculum planning, some institutions would seek views and feedback from the business community or the relevant trade associations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, we hope that the interaction between IHLs and trade associations will not be confined to merely consultation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In operationalising and implementing these training programmes, trade associations should also be invited to participate, particularly those which are willing and with the capabilities to do so.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The ability of our economy to sustain its growth is due partly to the business community and the Government-linked companies having sufficient top-rated talents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Taking this year's Budget as an example, the Government introduced the Net Investment Returns (NIR) framework in 2008.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The country's investment depends on high-quality talent, they possess global perspectives, rich industry experiences, and understand deeply global economic developments.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The fact that the NIR exceeds other tax revenues reflects the importance of high-end talent to our economy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI) has implemented many initiatives to study market developments in China and encouraging businesses across all sectors to broaden their vision.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: High-end talent can help businesses and industries to innovate and grow.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the long term, this will help contribute more towards our corporate income taxes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I suggest we undertake education with a broader perspective, and give more emphasis to the development of high-quality human resources, so as to promote the future development of our economy and businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is because the industry in those sectors may need more time to determine on the industry's future requirements.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Chairman, with the changing economy and technological disruptions, it is important for adult learners to continue to reskill and upskill themselves to face the needs of our future economy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: IHLs have been ramping up their delivery of CET, by providing short training courses for adults to acquire the right skills that can be applied in their respective jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: More industry-relevant modular courses have also been introduced to provide both undergraduates and postgraduates to learn new skills and develop deeper skills.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Beyond clearly skills-based and industry relevant courses, it is also important to continue support for postgraduate programmes like Masters programmes since they cater to a different group of Singaporeans who might prefer a more structured approach to training.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung had mentioned that MOE was going to review the funding for such postgraduate programmes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I am glad our autonomous universities (AUs) are following suit to keep up with the demand.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: These bite-sized courses are good for our busy individuals who are keen to upgrade and upskill themselves but do not have the time or resources for full-time postgraduate courses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The prestige and reputation of the AUs will give students further assurance of the effectiveness and legitimacy of the course materials and assessment methods.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Nevertheless, while the main goal of these micro-credentials is to encourage and recognise the mastery of specific skills, many individuals still aspire to attain formal postgraduate qualifications.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Will the Ministry expand the scheme and allow employees to eventually attain full qualifications from various micro-courses?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: For example, students who achieve sufficient micro-credentials in business administration topics could convert them into full credits and transfer them into a Bachelor’s Degree in Business Administration.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: According to Converge, a digital magazine by the Centre for Digital Education, which is a national research and advisory institute specialising in higher education technology trends, policy and funding, these are what universities in America are working on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We are gearing away from over-emphasis on academic accomplishments, but formal qualifications are still greatly valued and can be a powerful source of motivation for Singaporeans to pursue skills upgrading and lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Chairman, we are living in an increasingly interconnected world, and it is right and appropriate that our workforce reflect this global diversity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: However, back in 2013, I was surprised that Singaporean academics formed the minority in context-sensitive fields in political science, public policy and the communications departments in local universities.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: About a third of university academics in the UK are from outside the UK.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: This is according to figures published by the Higher Education Statistics Agency.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Saudi Arabia has gone down the localisation route, by hiring foreigners for academic positions at government universities as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The Minister had recognised the importance of academic staff diversity, in tandem with having our universities imbued with local character and identity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: With an eye on the latter, how confident is the Minister that the various talent and research schemes and platforms will result in a more equal footing in some key departments?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: What are some of the reasons this has happened and what is the impact that the Minister has noticed?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Do we know why some Singaporean academics find it hard to get to teach in local universities or why so few are tenured in local universities?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Can the Minister provide more clarity on these issues?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar, you can do the last cut for MOE.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as an Academic Board member of the Singapore Productivity and Standards Board (PSB) Academy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How does CPE plan to engage our students who are considering their post-secondary educational options to ensure they are aware of the expectations related to the different educational pathways and options available to them?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How does CPE plan to ensure that our PEIs remain responsible in offering quality and niche educational programmes for our students which have good employment outcomes, other than through the graduate employment survey or the EduTrust certification?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Would CPE consider carrying out surprise audits on the lecturers teaching in the PEIs to check on the quality of teaching and the qualifications of the lecturers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How does CPE plan to keep in check the fees of degree programmes offered by these PEIs to ensure they are not over-inflated?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Low Yen Ling and myself will try to answer all the cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have heard a lot about how the future will be different.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The questions from Ms Denise Phua, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Thomas Chua boil down to one central question that should really preoccupy every Education Minister in the world, and the question is: is our education system preparing young people for a fast-changing future, or is the model, as we know it, outdated?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is reflected in good PISA scores, good university rankings and good employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By no means they will guarantee success, but they are indicative of how we have gotten the evergreen basics right.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must build on, not sit on, this foundation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, this has been the mission of every single Education Minister in Singapore over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Forty years ago, our schools suffered from very high dropout rates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The uniform curriculum also did not cater for students’ varied pace of learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The then-Minister for Education, Dr Goh Keng Swee, said that the starting point is to identify the "causes of things", before putting in solutions to fix them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: His solution then was to allow students to study at different paces that suited them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Subsequent Education Ministers continued to tackle the problems of their times.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is due to all of them, and all our educators, that we have the strong foundation we have today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked for the worldwide trends we are grappling with now.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fact is that today, the Education Ministers face a challenge that is entirely different in nature compared to 40 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Things are changing so fast, and the future so dynamic, so volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA), that it is harder to identify the "causes of things" and come up with solutions before another future unfolds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, we can anticipate the shape of things to come and build a system that can respond to and embrace the changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can already identify some features of the future system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also need a new kind of IHL, where success is not measured merely by pass rates, employment outcomes or international rankings, but the long-term resilience of students, and their willingness to take risks, innovate and create.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By reshaping the education system, we can ensure the long-term prosperity of Singapore and continued social mobility across generations, an imperative of the education system that Ms Sylvia Lim raised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Denise Phua once told me – and she just repeated it again in her opening speech – that of all the changes made to the education system in recent years, the one that got her most excited was the integration of SkillsFuture Singapore into MOE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I remember in her words two years ago, she said it was "the game changer".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This change started IHLs breaking out of their traditional mould, from educating only students to becoming centres for lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The immediate impact is this: IHLs have started ramping up their courses for adult workers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the more profound impact is what is going to come next, which is their new approach to teaching.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because, previously, IHLs all had the mindset that we only have three to four years to prepare students before they embark on their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, from the word go, IHLs are in a race against time to pack in foundational knowledge, industry-related training, interdisciplinary skills and work attachments, all within those three to four years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The result is a hectic and technically very intensive curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Employers often comment that Singapore graduates know a lot of "stuff" – technical stuff.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we can do better in terms of soft skills, be genuinely interested in the industries we chose and the careers we chose, have some fire in our bellies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there is really no hurry to pack so much stuff into the formal curriculum in those three to four years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, there can be a greater focus on laying a strong foundation, giving them more time and space to seek counsel and decide on their career and their area of interest.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only an interest-driven choice will motivate students to want to learn their whole life, to master their professions and their crafts, and to build deep expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This paradigm shift will deeply affect the way education is delivered in IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will talk about three aspects today – Develop, Discover and Deepen.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Zainal Sapari said that the education model and techniques must be updated to reflect the changing needs of industry and the real world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why what our children are going through today at IHLs is vastly different from what we, as parents, went through when we were students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: IHLs can no longer merely be places to listen to lectures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Schools and IHLs must also be places where students make friends, build networks, seek mentorship, gain exposure to different cultures, discover what they want to do, and even find lifelong partners – but only at IHLs, not the schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In short, as Mr Edwin Tong pointed out, learning must become experiential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Knowledge no longer carries the same premium it used to because technology has made knowledge very accessible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What is highly valued today is how someone applies knowledge in real life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, what is valued is skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why all of our IHLs are introducing more experiential learning into their curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, industry attachments have become the norm, and practically all polytechnic students are required to go through them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At SIT, industry attachments are, in fact, an integral part of education, and last for up to a year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Internship is at one end of the spectrum of industry experience in IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the other end of the spectrum, which Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about, are various work-study programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The number is not big, but the number will grow, and the number of courses being offered will also grow.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also announced the launch of the ITE Work-Learn Technical Diploma in four sectors late last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A couple of Members asked for an update.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The technical courses are particularly popular, such as Marine and Offshore Engineering and Mechanical and Electrical Services Supervision.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, to Mr Thomas Chua's question on how do we bridge the gap between industry need and education, I call upon industries to participate directly in education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our new programmes are bringing industries into the IHLs, and IHLs into the industries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whether it is IHLs or industry, both can initiate the discussion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is also greater recognition of the importance of overseas exposure, because our young will very likely grow up to have to work in global industries and international environments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, around two-thirds of all AU students do at least one overseas stint, in the form of academic exchanges, overseas internships or entrepreneurship experiences, or short project-based trips.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SMU and SUTD are also focusing on exposing students to Southeast Asian countries which form Singapore's immediate economic hinterland.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In particular, overseas entrepreneurship programmes, where students are attached to startups in the US, Europe and Asia, are being ramped up rapidly in our AUs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Startup incubators, such as BLOCK71 and the Hangar at NUS, NTUitive at NTU, as well as Pollinate, jointly set up by Ngee Ann Polytechnic, Singapore Polytechnic and Temasek Polytechnic, are all buzzing with activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Experiential learning also involves learning knowledge and skills that are contemporary, relevant and hands-on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At NUS, there is a strong emphasis on data science and IT.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All students, whether you are learning Literature, Arts, History, Science or Engineering, must take compulsory modules on either quantitative reasoning or computational thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are the foundational skills to coding and data analytics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: NTU, too, has announced that it will make courses in digital literacy compulsory for all students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a significant shift in IHL curriculum, and it has taken off across the board.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I visited our local engineering company, HOPE Technik, recently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members will know them for building the Red Rhinos for our Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are also building robots, autonomous vehicles and exoskeletons for many international customers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I asked how we can improve the education of engineers, one of the founders, Mr Peter Ho, an NUS alumnus, said that engineering students should learn how to weld.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He said knowing welding means you can do prototyping, and that makes you a better engineer.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think there is a lot of wisdom in that comment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It reflects a growing need to incorporate innovation and creativity into our curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is Applied Learning right there, as Minister Ng Chee Meng spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am not sure if, in time, our engineering students will all learn welding, but they do learn 3D printing today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And perhaps all engineering students should learn prototyping.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The practice of IHLs today frontloading education and packing a lot of stuff into the first few years is most stark in our polytechnics, where students are funnelled into occupation-specific courses right from the start.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over time, courses also proliferated as employers wanted graduates with specialised skills and wanted them fast.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But it is daunting and confusing for our young students, who, at the age 16 or 17, have to choose amongst 230 courses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most of them hardly know what work life is like, much less the work nature in these specific jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As IHLs transform into centres for lifelong learning, this approach will change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, we will have more Common Entry Programmes (CEPs) at the polytechnics, which Mr Seah Kian Peng asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While there is always a small group of students who are very clear about what they want to do from a very young age, the majority of students will be in a self-discovery mode when entering polytechnics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They may have an idea that they like engineering, IT or social science, but find it too early to pick a course that is specific to an occupation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For these students, therefore, I agree with Mr Seah Kian Peng that giving them more time to explore their interests will help.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CEPs comprise foundational modules common to a particular cluster of discipline, and students get to sample all of them and explore their interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To illustrate, for a student in the Information and Digital Technologies cluster, he will take foundational courses in Computing Mathematics, Introduction to Programming and Networking Fundamentals in his first year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From his second year, he then decides on his specialisation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over-specificity puts students at greater risk of being displaced when the industry changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It can also stifle the versatility of students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By streamlining the course choices for students, we increase the career options for graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are consciously trading depth for more breadth and versatility.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is no fall in polytechnic intake due to this change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The two changes I just spoke about need to be supplemented with a stronger and more systemic effort to guide students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has to start in secondary schools to help students get a broad sense of where their interests and strengths lie.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is where Applied Learning will really help.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Typically, this falls into one of the following four domains – science and technology, ICT, social sciences and humanities, or the creative arts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the IHLs, the process will continue to, first, expose students to knowledge and skills within their chosen cluster of disciplines, and then to help them identity their specialisation later on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Towards the tail end of their IHL education, they will undergo industry attachment – like a capstone – to reaffirm their interest in their chosen career.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a systemic, self-discovery approach for students, which we will roll out to all the IHLs in the coming year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Stronger ECG ensures that more students can navigate the multiple education pathways available and choose the one most suitable for them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One such pathway is the Polytechnic Foundation Programme (PFP) which Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To give Members some background, today, polytechnics mostly admit students who graduated with the GCE "O" level certificate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They also take in a small group of students who graduated with Normal (Academic), or N(A), certificates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These students from the N(A) stream did well for their GCE "N" level examinations and are given a chance to go directly to the polytechnics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We started PFP in 2013 and the first batch just graduated in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The outcomes have been very encouraging, and maybe even surprising to some.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Typically, 25% of every cohort scores a Grade Point Average (GPA) of 3.5 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But for PFP students, 35% achieved it – 35% compared to 25% on average.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The norm is that 55% of each cohort score GPA 3 and above, but 70% of PFP students achieved it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dropout rates for PFP students are also much lower than average.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They said being offered PFP greatly motivated the N(A) students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I also believe that it has something to do with the students' strong interest in the polytechnic path that they chose.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is an important lesson in education policy here.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Given the right encouragement and a chance to prove themselves, especially in an area that they enjoy doing, the students will do their best and will have a good chance of doing well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This inner drive outweighs all the tuition and all the close supervision that are given to the students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, PFP is open to students from the GCE "N" level stream who score an aggregate of 11 points and below.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With this change, the number of students accepted every year will increase from about 1,200 today to 1,500.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, our IHLs' admission processes consider factors beyond academic accomplishments to recognise students who have already discovered their interests and aptitudes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: NUS just announced that it will give bonus points for first choice applications to encourage students to pursue their interests and I really commend them for that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Polytechnic principals told me that since I announced and implemented that, they have been receiving many more appeals from students and parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is expected, and I thank the IHLs for looking at every single appeal carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What students and parents need to understand is that passion and aptitude need to be demonstrated and is not declared, and that has to come through during the admission process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, during my time, if a child likes airplanes, he would know every model of airplanes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He would go to Changi Airport as a past-time to see airplanes take off and land.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And he would have the digital video disc (DVD) of "Top Gun" and would have watched it 20 times.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This interest is demonstrated, and you cannot hide it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, there is scope for us to do more at ITE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ideally, admission to vocational training pathways should predominantly be aptitude-based.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are practical constraints, such as course capacity or the industries' ability to absorb these graduates, but where possible, we want every student to enter a vocation of his liking.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I also note Ms Denise Phua's two examples of students from the GCE "N" level stream who like art but were unable to get into LaSalle or NAFA, and that is because they require a minimum of GCE "O" level certificates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After all, we have PFP programmes that allow students from the "N" level stream to go to a Diploma programme in polytechnics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we will review that, and I thank the Member for the feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Next, let me talk about deepening what we learn through lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked about the status and future plans of SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SkillsFuture is not just the SkillsFuture Credit as we all know.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Neither is it just about getting IHLs to deliver training programmes for adults.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It requires a transformation of the education system as we know it; it requires our young to uncover their interests and passions and commit to learning their whole life; it requires employers, private training providers and IHLs to all do their part for lifelong learning; it requires society to celebrate and recognise a broad range of achievements and success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: IHLs can play a bigger role in our future plans for SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have studied the ITMs, gotten feedback from industry partners, and have launched around 800 industry-relevant modular courses since October last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are collectively known as the SkillsFuture Series and cover a wide range of disciplines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ICT is a key focus of the IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is value for each IHL to contribute.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There will be some overlap, but I do not think it is a problem so long as the demand is strong.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And over time, each IHL will find its niche and the landscape will settle.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These courses are funded at up to 70% upfront, so that fees are significantly lower.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many will be structured as Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs), where funding will be even more generous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As of February this year, more than 4,900 adult learners have enrolled in SkillsFuture Series courses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The IHLs will develop more modular courses in the coming year and sharpen their focus to meet industry's evolving needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the IHLs roll out more modular courses, the AUs will repackage certain courses to create pathways that lead to smaller qualifications, often referred to as "micro-credentials".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These micro-credentials comprise only modules targeted at developing expertise for work and, as Dr Lim Wee Kiak said, can be useful in providing a milestone for adult learners to aim towards and which employers can recognise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, we should be careful not to let such micro-credentials become a new arms race to collect credentials.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: IHLs should instead focus on imparting skills and knowledge needed by industry and package them into a nice bundle that represents a meaningful upgrading of skills and know-how.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Learners, too, should focus on picking up what is necessary for their work and for their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our AUs will progressively roll out more of such micro-credentials in the coming years and subject them to the market test.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we step up support for SkillsFuture Series courses, we also reviewed the way we fund Postgraduate by Coursework programmes at our universities, namely, Master's by Coursework and Postgraduate Diplomas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Miss Cheng Li Hui asked for an update on the review.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Given our limited budget, we need to do some re-allocation of resources.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, from 2019, for the majority of MOE-funded Postgraduate by Coursework programmes, the subsidy level for Permanent Residents (PRs) will be adjusted slightly downwards, while that for international students will be discontinued.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, there will be no change in the subsidy level for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will free up around $25 million in budget each year, which will be rechannelled to support modular courses at our IHLs for our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding the reduction in subsidy for non-Singaporeans, we must continue to attract selected, deserving postgraduate international students who can make meaningful contributions to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Besides these discrete changes, what is more important is the shift in the mindsets of all of our IHLs to embrace lifelong learning as part of their mission.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng is right that gone are the days where a degree can last someone a lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: NUS is blazing the trail in this regard.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The response was overwhelming, and alumni started to attend classes side by side with young undergraduates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will help their students build their careers and learn for life during this period.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This gives new meaning to the word "alumni".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am sure this change in mindset will spread to all IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, short courses for adults are mostly unpacked from long full-time programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In time, they will have to be developed independently, with a practical bent – delivered by practitioners on skills in demand by industries; or a futuristic bent – taught by researchers on cutting-edge technology.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Transformation of education cannot be done by MOE alone.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I agree with Ms Foo Mee Har that a key partner in education are the employers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the best reward for them is the outcome of their investment in their own people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we shift the IHL system to lay a stronger foundation for students and be less prescriptive in the occupation we are preparing them for, employers need to step up even more to involve themselves in education and lifelong learning, especially for the young.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also need to work closely with the most important people in our students' lives – their parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our children are often the people we love the most.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is natural for parents to want to bring them up impeccably – from the night feeds when they are babies, helping them with homework when they are in primary school, taking leave when they are taking PSLE, attending Open Houses at the IHLs with them, interviewing their boyfriends and girlfriends.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the truth is we are all parents-in-training.
